PROLOGUE

If one considers carefully the evangelical and apostolic preaching, one will find
quite clearly that the preaching of the Catholic preachers must deal with vices
and virtues: persuading toward one and dissuading from the other. And most continually it must be
to persuade them toward the theological virtues, and dissuade them from the vices contrary
to these (and on this there is much material in the first six books of this history; and
in the postil on the epistles and gospels for the Sundays of the whole year, which I
made; and much more fully in the Christian Doctrine, which the first twelve
preachers preached to this Indian people, which I, as an eyewitness,
compiled in this Mexican language). And in order to give greater opportunity and help
to the preachers of this new Church, in this volume I have dealt with the
moral virtues according to the understanding, practice, and language that these same people
have of them. I have not followed in this treatise the order that other writers have used
in treating this subject matter, but instead follow the order of the persons, dignities, and offices
and occupations that exist among this people, setting forth the goodness of each person and then
their wickedness, with an abundance of nouns, adjectives, and verbs (where there is great
abundance of language very proper and very common among them). There are also
contained, in this same style, in this volume, all the parts of the body, both
internal and external, in great detail; and after this, most of the illnesses
to which human bodies are subject in this land, and the remedies
against them; and along with this, nearly all the generations that have come
to settle this land.

of the tenth book.

Here begins the tenth book of the General History, in which are treated the vices and virtues, both spiritual and corporal, of every kind of person.

Chapter One, on the qualities and conditions of persons related by kinship.

The father is the first root and stock of kinship. The proper quality of a good father is to be diligent and careful, that with perseverance he maintain his household and sustain it.
The good father rears and maintains his children, gives them a good upbringing and instruction, corrects them, gives them good examples and good counsel, and stores up treasure for them, and keeps watch over them; he keeps account of the expenses of his household, and regulates his children's spending, and provides for things to come.

The quality of a bad father is to be lazy, careless, idle; he looks after no one, he lacks the diligence to do what he is obliged to do, and he wastes his time in vain.

[fo. 1]

Here is the tenth book, which treats of the General History: here are told the various virtues, both good and evil, and all the vices and good customs that are practiced, and by these our hearts are known — whoever does them.

Here is the first chapter, in which is told the manner and condition of life of those who are joined together by ties of blood kinship.

The father, the parent, is the true root of kinship, the origin of lineage; he is the heart of the father's line; he is one who receives, who loves, who is attentive, who is anxious, who is burdened, who worries, who is responsible, who cares for others.

He rears, he nurtures, he raises up, he teaches, he admonishes, he instructs, he guides the life of his children; he sets up a bright mirror for them, he holds before them a great burning torch; he is attentive, he corrects, he disciplines, he watches over, he is mindful, he is prudent, he looks far ahead, he is thoughtful, he settles matters, he puts things in order.

As for the bad father, the negligent one, the lazy one: he does not care for anyone, he is thoughtless, he is careless, he does no good for his children, he abandons them, he neglects them, he lets things go undone, he leaves them forsaken.

Book Ten

The quality proper to the mother is
to have children, and give them milk; the
virtuous mother is watchful and quick, she does not
stop, she is diligent, a watcher, solicitous and
anxious. She raises her children, is continually
caring for them, has vigilance, lacks nothing,
she pampers them, she is like a light for
everyone in her house, she becomes anxious
over the needs of each one, and no
necessary thing in the house is neglected;
she is a keeper of order, she is industrious, or
hard-working.

The bad mother is foolish, ignorant,
sleepy, lazy, wasteful,
a person of poor management, careless
of her house, she lets things be lost
through laziness or anger; she does not attend to
the needs of those in her house, she does not
look after the things of her house, she does not
correct the faults of those in her house: and for
that reason she grows worse every day —.

[image: a swaddled infant, with the sun]

Among these people there are legitimate
children, and bastard children.

[image: two figures with a child]

A well-conditioned, or virtuous, child.
The well-conditioned child is obedient,
humble, grateful,
reverent, and imitates his parents in

The mother — she who is a mother, who has children,
who nurses them well, of good heart, watchful,
diligent, quick, wakeful,
patient of heart, cautious.
She raises her children strictly, cares for them
completely, she makes things well for them,
she watches over them, she does not neglect them,
she is attentive, she looks after them.

The bad mother is wicked,
not good; she is a deceiver of appearances, foolish,
drowsy, careless, she causes
things to be lost, she hides things from people, she
bewitches people's belongings, she makes people
lose things, she is negligent, she is
lazy, she is ill-tempered, she cares for nothing
properly, she does not attend
to anything, she does not do her duty,
she does not look after things,
she causes people to fall into pits, into ravines, she
makes others suffer, she treats rabbits
and deer like playthings, she shows them
to others, she lets things be scattered, cast about,
and mixed up.

The child, the offspring, the child
of a nobleman, within the house is a child
of the household, by birth a legitimate child.

A hidden child (illegitimate), a child of the
household, a child of the house, a child
born of a rope-maker, a child of low station.

The good child is one who respects people,
who is humble, who is modest,
who is grateful, who honors
others, who shows reverence, who treats people well

Of vices and virtues.

Customs, and in body, a child resembles his father or his mother.

The vicious son.

The bad son is mischievous, rebellious, or disobedient, crazy, mischievous, unreceptive to good counsel; he throws good doctrine behind his back; he is restless, dissolute, boastful, vainglorious, ill-bred, uncouth or rough; he receives no good teaching. The good counsels of his father and his mother go in one ear and out the other; even if he is whipped, and even if he is beaten, he does not for that reason mend his ways.

The virtuous daughter.

The young woman or daughter who is raised in her father's house has these good qualities: she is truly a virgin, never known by a man; she is obedient, modest, intelligent, able; a noble woman, honored, respected, well brought up, instructed, taught; a person who is advised, warned, and kept watch over.

And virtues. Folio 2.

[Continuing from the previous page] ...she is trustworthy, discreet, generous, good-hearted, gracious; she makes things known to others, she visits and speaks with people.

The vicious child, the wretched son, is utterly wretched, stubborn, hard-hearted, of evil heart, wretched of heart, hollow-headed, deaf to advice, wayward, wide-eyed with fright, foolish, proud, muddled, one who must constantly be talked to and corrected, foolish, ungrateful, taking nothing to heart, neither his mother's nor his father's words. He goes about causing trouble on every side; he thrusts his hand even into the ears of those who try to raise and discipline him; he is like a stinging nettle wherever he looks; no one respects him; he lives frivolously, he lives restlessly, he opens his eyes wide in mischief, he mocks things, he twists things about, he perverts things.

The modest young woman, the reared maiden, the well-brought-up maiden, who truly is a maiden in body and soul — she is good, virtuous; a good maiden is obedient, discreet, attentive, prudent, of good understanding, dignified, respectable, worthy of honor and fear, well counseled, well reared, well taught, well instructed, of pure and good life, modest.

Folio 4.

Book Ten

The vicious daughter.

The bad or wicked daughter is bad in her body: dissolute, loose, a whore, over-dressed, she goes about showing off, adorning herself with excessive care, wandering through the streets, giving herself over to the vices of the flesh; she goes about like a flower picked at the roadside — her whole life and pleasure consists of wandering like a weed by the wayside; she goes about like a madwoman.

Spoiled son or daughter.

A boy or girl who takes after his or her family's lineage, noble or generous — a delicate, pampered, tender, and beautiful daughter.
The eldest daughter is called the firstborn; the second daughter; the third daughter; the last daughter. The prudent reader should not take offense that only words, and not full sentences, are given here, as was done above; in other parts further on [sentences will be given], because the main purpose of this treatise is to apply the Castilian language to the Indian language, so that people may learn to speak the proper words concerning this subject of vices and virtues.

A virtuous boy or girl.

A boy or girl of good character is diligent, lively, sharp-witted, quick, moderate, discreet, and obedient, who willingly does what he is told.

A vicious boy.

The wicked boy has these traits: he is lazy, slow, fat and clumsy, foolish, stupid, coarse, and indiscreet, understanding things backwards.

[The Nahuatl text on the right presents the same subject matter in the Nahuatl language — listing the corresponding terms and descriptions for "wicked daughter," "spoiled child," "virtuous child," and "vicious child," paralleling the Spanish text at left with the equivalent Nahuatl vocabulary for laziness, mischievousness, diligence, obedience, and related qualities.]

Of vices

He does things backwards, unskilled, if
they are such, foolish, mad, always
going from house to house, from place
to place, a refined rascal, or sick with
all manner of illnesses.

Uncle.
¶These natives had as a custom, concerning the uncle,
to leave him as guardian or tutor of his
nephews, and of his estate, and of his wife, and
of the whole household. ¶The faithful uncle took
charge of the house of his brother
and sister-in-law, as if it were
his own.

Bad uncle.
¶The characteristic of a bad uncle
is to be wasteful, dissolute,
disdainful, and contemptuous.

Aunt.
¶The aunt tends to be the supporter
and protector of her nephews and nieces.
The good aunt is merciful, favors
her kin, continually takes care
of her own, has a noble disposition,
and is diligent in seeking what is
necessary for her relatives.

Bad aunt.
¶The aunt who is of bad disposition
is fierce, easily angered,
sour-faced; no one feels
comfortable with her; she is distant,
always looking with ill will, esteeming
everyone but little, looking with
disdain or scorn.

Nephew, or niece
¶In one way the men call them...

¶The uncle is one who is relied upon by his nephews,
one in whom trust is placed, one who gives counsel,
one who corrects, who governs, who rules wisely.
¶The good uncle becomes angry [for good reason], he makes people prudent,
he receives [his kin] well, he watches over them, he guards them, through him
one becomes fit to live rightly; he is feared,
he acts with proper fear; he makes people prudent, he causes sorrow [for their faults] out of care.

¶The bad uncle is one who makes a mockery of others,
who causes others to be mocked, who exposes others to ridicule,
who scorns others, who ruins others, who hates people, who looks
upon others with contempt, who despises them.

¶The aunt, likewise the aunts. ¶The
good aunt is compassionate of heart, merciful,
she speaks on behalf of others, she receives them kindly, she
holds them dear in her heart, she loves her kin, she loves them
dearly, she takes care of them, she feels concern for others.

¶The bad aunt is bitter of heart,
foul-hearted, bad-tempered, sharp-tongued,
of harsh speech, quarrelsome, she
desires nothing good, she regards others with hatred, she looks on them
with anger, she despises them, she regards them with disdain.

¶Nephew, the one who is nephew to someone, one's nephew.

Book Ten

[Continued from previous page] ...who has good judgment, is a man of good
example, and of good doctrine, who leaves behind
a good reputation, of good renown, who
leaves works of good memory in life,
in property, and in lineage, written
as if in a book.

The bad great-grandfather is like a rotten
wall, like a corner, like darkness,
worthy of sermons, worthy
of being reprehended or scolded, worthy
of being mocked, worthy that those
who live murmur against him; where he is
in hell, they mock him, and all
spit upon him: his memory or his sight
causes pain or anger.

Great-grandmother.

The great-grandmother is a figure of old age,
she is like a child in her condition: the good
great-grandmother is worthy of being praised,
worthy that one be grateful to her for the good
she did for her descendants; it is a glory
to her descendants to be named
after her, as great-grandmother, for she is the origin
of the lineage or family line. The bad great-
grandmother is detestable; no one willingly hears
her name, her presence
or her memory provokes nausea or disgust,
and causes anger.

Great-great-grandfather.
The great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother tremble
in the head, and the body is always
coughing, walks bent over, grows weak,
and is at the very end of old age. The good
great-great-grandfather, or great-great-grandmother, stands in
the place of father and mother to their descendants,
is like a precious root or foundation.
The bad great-great-grandfather, or great-great-grandmother, is
a worthless old person, a worthless root, cast aside, who lived a
bad life, leaving his or her own with nothing good to remember.

[Nahuatl column, parallel text describing the same concepts of ancestors — great-grandparents, their qualities both good and bad, their role as root and origin of lineage, the respect or contempt they may receive, and the physical decline of extreme old age — rendered in Nahuatl terms such as "tlaueliloc" (wicked), "qualli" (good), "ilama" (old woman), and "nelhuaiotl" (root), corresponding thematically to the Spanish text at left.]

Of the vices
Grandson or granddaughter.
¶The grandson or granddaughter is loved, is
cherished, is esteemed; he proceeds
from his ancestors, like the thorns
on which one is born, or like the chips
left from the stone that is carved, or like
the kernels of the ear of corn, the adopted one
called "cacamatl," a crumb,
alive, precious, like a precious stone,
like fine plumage; imitators
of their own kin, in bearing and in
deeds. The good grandson follows the
good examples of his own people; he is
a living image of them, he brings
honor to his own, with his good
life he blossoms like a flower among
his own. The mischievous grandson
dishonors his own, scatters to dust
the honor of his own: he is dissolute
and self-willed, takes no one's
opinion on what he must
say; he governs himself however he
pleases, judges as he fancies,
he is conceited, villainous, and utterly arrogant.

Chapter two, on the
degrees of affinity.
Father-in-law.
¶The father-in-law is he who has
a son-in-law or daughter-in-law; if they are living (so called); if they are dead,
he is called "miccamontatli."
The father-in-law seeks out a wife for
his son, and marries off his daughters, and
takes care of his grandchildren.
The good father-in-law takes care to
give his son-in-law what he needs,
and to settle his daughter-in-law in
his house.
The bad father-in-law always holds hatred
toward his daughter-in-law or his son, between his
daughter and his son-in-law; he wants no one
to stay in his house — he is stingy, miserly.

And virtues.
Folio 5.
¶He is a grandchild, a beloved child, his hair, his fingernail,
his beard, his eyebrow, his thorn-bramble, his covering,
his shell, his leftover kernel, his remnant,
his heritage, a jewel, a precious feather, one brought forth.
¶The good grandchild resembles his grandparent, is his likeness,
gives him glory, gives him splendor, he blossoms,
he opens like a flower. ¶As for the unfortunate grandchild: he
squanders things, he destroys things,
he ruins things, he dishonors things, he disgraces
things, he brings death to people, he vexes others' hearts,
he troubles others' spirits, he harms the helpless, he
creates nothing for anyone, he indulges only himself, he carries
himself as he wishes, he governs himself, he only
judges for himself, he heeds no one,
he thinks only of his own interest, he befriends only himself, he makes his own
rules.

DEGREE OF AFFINITY
¶Father-in-law, deceased father-in-law, mother-in-law,
son-in-law, one who takes a son-in-law, one who takes a daughter-in-law,
one who gives a daughter in marriage. He seeks, he looks for,
he arranges marriages, he arranges marriages. The good father-in-law
loves people, he establishes a household for them, he embraces them,
he takes them into his arms. The bad, unfortunate father-in-law is one who
sows discord between people, who divides them,
who scatters them about; no one wants him near, he is stingy, quarrelsome.
7

Book Ten

Mother-in-law.
The mother-in-law does, on her part, for her children, everything that was said about the father-in-law. The good mother-in-law watches over her daughter-in-law and guards her discreetly. The bad mother-in-law rejoices if her daughter-in-law is of poor account, is a waster of her own and others' property, and is unfaithful to her daughter-in-law.

Father of the father-in-law.
The honored father, or father of the father-in-law, has all the qualities that were said of the father-in-law. The good lord is rich and has gained much through his labor. The bad lord-father, or poor one, is stingy, useless, and never leaves his corner.

Mother of the father-in-law, or mother-in-law.
The honored mother, mother of the father-in-law or mother-in-law, has the same qualities as the mother-in-law. The good honored mother is an old, honored, lovable, and venerable woman. The bad honored mother harms herself and her family, leaving debts that her successors must later pay.

Son-in-law.
The son-in-law is a young married man, exempt from the order of the tlamacazque and telpuchtli. The good son-in-law is respectful, reverent, and loved by his parents-in-law. The bad son-in-law is shameless, grasping, or covetous; he steals what he can from his father-in-law's house and lives in concubinage.

Daughter-in-law.
The daughter-in-law is formally requested in marriage, a legitimate wife; the good daughter-in-law is not gossipy

[Nahuatl text describing the qualities of mother-in-law (monnantli), father-in-law (moncutli), son-in-law/husband relations (monatli, montli), and daughter-in-law (cioamontli) — paralleling the Spanish descriptions: the good mother-in-law watches over and cares for her kin, respects and serves them; the bad one mistreats and shames them. The good father-in-law is diligent, possesses property, and works hard; the bad one is poor, suffers, and lives miserably. The good husband (monatli) is precious, beloved, feared, and respected; the bad husband strikes his wife, gambles, and abandons his responsibilities. The good husband (montli) is honored, respectful, and faithful; the bad one is foolish, wasteful, dissolute, and promiscuous. The daughter-in-law, when good... [continues]]

she bears reprimands with patience,
loves and pampers, and flatters

The ill-conditioned daughter-in-law
is argumentative, and quarrelsome, wrathful,
choleric, fierce, she is furious,

Brother-in-law.

¶ A brother-in-law should be of a gentle,
mild disposition, hardworking,
a skilled craftsman, kind, and straightforward.
An ill-conditioned brother-in-law is
envious, resentful, he becomes angry,

The elder brother leads the household of his father; he instructs his younger siblings, relieving them of work until they are of age to work.

Stepfather
The stepfather is one who marries a woman widowed by another husband, who left sons or daughters: these he takes as his stepchildren; yet he is steadfast in his labors. The bad stepfather abhors his stepchildren, cannot bear the sight of them, and wishes them dead.

Stepmother
The stepmother is she who marries a man who has children by another woman. A stepmother of good character treats her stepchildren with love, favors them, and gives them gifts. An ill-tempered stepmother is fierce, spiteful, sour-faced, and always looks upon them with angry eyes.

Stepchildren.

This name, tlacatl, means to say a noble, generous, or magnificent person; and its compound, atlacatl, is its opposite, signifying a vile person of low condition. And the compounds of tlacatl formed with numbers signify a common person: thus, saying catlacatl means one person, man or woman; ome tlacatl, two persons, men or women. And saying cuix tlacatl means it is a vile, low person; and when they say cacanca tlacatl, they mean a very good, very noble, or very generous person.

The excellences of the lord king or emperor, bishop, or pope are expressed by way of metaphor. Ceoallo, hecauhio means a thing that gives shade, because the greater one must give shade to his subjects. Malacayo is a thing that takes great care in giving shade, because the greater one must shelter all, small and great. Puchotl is a tree that gives great shade and has many branches. Aueuetl is of the same kind, for the lord must be like these trees, under which all his subjects find shelter. The great one must be revered, awe-inspiring, esteemed, and feared by all. The great one who performs his office well must carry his subjects — some on his back, others in his lap, others in his arms — gathering them and keeping them under his wings, as a hen does her chicks.

The senator has these qualities: namely, to be a judge, to know how to investigate lawsuits well, to be respected...

If she is bad, she is reckless, troublesome, disruptive, and restless, such that for no reason she tends to threaten, and inspire great fear and dread in everyone, and is so fierce that she seems as if she would eat the others alive.

Such a one, if good, rules her subjects very well, and punishes the bad ones; she is respected, makes laws, and gives order in whatever is needed, and is obeyed in everything.

The one who is bad is careless and lax, lets things be lost through negligence, and is given to exaggeration, and in everything sets a bad example, and puts things at peril and risk, and is very scandalous.

The one who sells honey has maguey plants, and usually sells a local wine made from the honey of the maguey, which he first cooks, boiling it. And because the honey is never lacking, he usually plants the offshoots of the magueys, and after they have grown, he digs, or hollows out, their core. And once hollowed, he scrapes them well so that the honey, from which he makes pulque, may flow, cooking it or boiling it first, and then fills jars or skins with it to store it; this is done once they have roots.

The honey he sells is thick — so thick that it seems curdled, very sweet, tasty — and at times he sells the kind that scrapes the throat: sour, or it tastes watery, seeming like plain water.

The good dealer in this trade does not adulterate the honey with anything; rather, since it is pure, he sells it as such, whether it be bee honey or of another kind, white or dark. After having written about the abilities and trades that these native Mexicans had in the time of their unbelief (paganism), and the vices and virtues that were held among them: it seemed to me reasonable to set down here the trades, abilities, vices and virtues that they have since acquired. As to the first point: we know from experience that in mechanical trades, they are skillful at learning and using them in the manner the Spaniards know and practice them: such as the trades of geometry, that is, building, which they understand and carry out just as the Spaniards do—

...which is within, and which is on the outside, it is thus in our [bodies], in our male and female [nature]...

An experiment was also made with women, to see whether, just as in the time of idolatry there had been convents of them who served in the temples and kept chastity and were suited to becoming nuns and religious women of the Christian faith, keeping perpetual chastity. For this purpose convents and congregations of women were established, and they were instructed in spiritual matters, and many of them learned to read and write, and those who seemed to us well instructed in the faith were matrons of good judgment; we made them superiors over the others, so that they might govern and teach them in the matters of Christianity and in all good customs. Indeed, at the beginning we held the opinion that the men would be fit to become priests and religious, and the women to become nuns and religious women. But our opinion deceived us: through experience we came to understand that at that time they were not capable of such perfection; and thus the congregation and convents that we had attempted at the beginning ceased, nor even now do we see signs that this undertaking can be achieved.

The labors and difficulties we had at the beginning were great, in order to marry those who had been baptized; for they had many wives, and we had to give them the one that the law commands they should take, because in order to examine the degrees of kinship and know which was the first wife, so as to give her to him—we found ourselves in a labyrinth of great difficulty, because they would lie about which was the first wife, and would invent deceits in order to marry the one they were most fond of, and in order to learn with which one they had performed the ceremony that was used when taking a legitimate wife. It was necessary to investigate thoroughly and learn many ceremonies and idolatrous rites of their infidelity, and since we knew little of the language, we almost never properly grasped the matter, as we now understand it. Concerning the other sacraments, such as confession and communion, there has been so much difficulty in establishing them on their proper footing that even now there are very few who go directly to receive these sacraments, which causes us great weariness and gives us much insight into how little progress has been made in Christianity.

...cotitlan: which now bears the name of Tula, from having dwelt and lived there together; to this day there are signs of the many works they made there. Among these they left one work that still stands there and can be seen today, although they did not finish it, called coatlaquetzalli: these are pillars shaped like serpents, with the head resting on the ground as a foot, and the tail and rattles above. They also left a mountain, or a hill, that the said Toltecs began to build and never finished, and the old foundations of their houses and the plasterwork can still be seen today. Also found today are objects they first made: namely, pieces of pots or clay vessels, bowls, and jars. Likewise, jewels and precious stones, emeralds, and fine turquoises are dug up from beneath the earth.

All these so-called Toltecs were called Chichimecs, and had no other particular name except the one they took from the skill and refinement of the works they made, by which they came to be called Toltecs — as if we were to say "refined and skillful craftsmen," like the Flemish are considered today. And rightly so, because they were subtle and accomplished in whatever they put their hands to, for everything was very fine, exquisite, and graceful, like the very curious things they made...

[Nahuatl column — parallel account describing the Toltecs' works and craftsmanship: it tells how they made many fine things, crafted and finished various objects, and left behind structures such as the serpent-pillars (coatlaquetzalli), round pillars, stepped platforms, and carved stone walls. It continues that potsherds, carved stones, and remnants of their buildings can still be found, and that from the earth are also recovered Toltec necklaces, bracelets, precious jewels, jade, turquoise, and fine green stones (quetzalitztli).

It goes on to explain that the Toltecs were also called Chichimecs, though they had no distinct separate name of their own; rather, their name came from their own nature, their way of life, and their works. Thus they were called "toltecatl" (artisan), meaning wise, skillful, excellent in everything they made — all their works were good, fine, and admirable; their houses were well built, well carved, well finished, truly marvelous. For whatever a Toltec made — whether a house or a finely wrought object — was always carefully crafted and skillfully fashioned, for such was their special occupation and their proper task.]

[These were houses] that were adorned inside with a certain kind of very green precious stones, in place of plaster, and the other houses that were not so adorned had a very polished plaster surface, pleasant to see, and the stones of which they were made were also carved and also inlaid, so that it seemed to be mosaic work; and thus they were rightly called "houses of skilled and curious craftsmen," for having such beauty of refinement and workmanship. There was also a temple, belonging to their priest called Quetzalcoatl, much more polished and precious than their own houses.

It had four chambers: one faced east, and was of gold, and they called it the "golden chamber," or "golden house," because instead of plaster it had gold in sheets, very finely fastened. The defects, or faults, of the Otomis.

The Otomis by nature were clumsy, coarse, and inept, and because of their clumsiness people would say, as an insult, "you are inept, you are like an Otomi," meaning that you fail to understand what is told to you. Perhaps you are even one of the actual Otomis: in truth you are not even their equal, but are entirely and purely an Otomi — and even more so than an Otomi. All of this was said as an insult to one who is inept and clumsy, reproaching him for his lack of capacity and ability.

Of the quaquatas, matlatzincas, toloques. Folio 131

The reason they are called "quata" when it is one, and "quaquatas" when there are many, is because they always carry their heads girded with the sling: for which reason the word is said to come from "qua," an abbreviation that means to say "quaitl," which is the head, and "ta," which means to say "tematlatl," which is the sling: and thus it means to say "quatatl": a man who carries the sling on his head, by way of a sling-cord. It is also interpreted another way, meaning: a man with a head of stone.

[illustration of three figures with slings]

These so-called Quaquatas, as in their own land—which is the valley they call Matlatzinco—it is extremely cold there: they tend to be hardy, and fit for much labor: and as they used slings, with which they did harm from afar, with them they were very bold and determined, and ill-regarded: both in peace and in war: for which reason, one who is ill-regarded and of little respect, to insult him, they say to him: "he looks quite like a quata," as one would say, ill-bred or reckless: and likewise the strong wine, which would immediately go to their heads.

[The Nahuatl text, parallel to the Spanish, explains:] "Quatatl" — thus the many "quaquata" are so named, because they always carry about with them, always bound to themselves, the sling upon the head; thus it is said, "quatematle" — upon the head; it is said "tzontecomatl," the head, is called "tatl," the sling; thus it is said "quatematle," or it is said "quate quatatl," thus the stone upon the head is called "stone-of-the-head."

These Quaquata, in their home, in their land, called Matlatzinco: it is very cold there, therefore they are very strong, ruddy, robust, sturdy — these quaquata: and for this reason the sling is sent to strike from afar: therefore they are also very fierce upon the earth and in war: and he who is not prudent, who sleeps carelessly before others, is said to be called "Quatatl," and it is said, thus like a "quata."
